sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Fairies are the supernatural beings of the Celtic world whom folk tradition keeps apart from the human community. Their shapes and names change from one country to the next, yet the same ideas recur in the tales. They dwell in a hidden world of their own, they may help or harm humans, and they are close to the dead and to the earth. The old tales say much about who the fairies are. Some say they are the souls of the dead, held in a kind of waiting place and set apart from the living. Others hold that they are a separate people who once shared the land with humans and then drew away into the hollow hills. The tales of the fairy mound and of time spent within it are many. MacKillop's Dictionary notes that the earliest written fairy lore comes from the learned writers of the Middle Ages, such as Giraldus Cambrensis. Yet most of it reached the page from modern oral tradition. Each tongue keeps its own word for the fairy, and there is no single term common to all of the Celtic lands. So there is no one unified Celtic fairy tradition at all. Fairies can help the household. They set the work of the house in order, they guard the cattle, and they reward the kind. But they have a dark side. A human who eats the fairy food or spends the night in their company may find years have gone by in a few hours. A chill or a faint may be blamed on a fairy stroke, and a sick child might have been taken by the fairies and another left in its place, a changeling. If crossed, a fairy will take sharp revenge, and common punishments are a burning house and spoiled crops. People guard against them with iron, with rowan and with a pierced stone. Green was their colour, so some kept green from the clothing. They were spoken of with care, and warily, as the Good People or the fair family, lest the name itself bring their anger. Each country keeps its own fairy. In Ireland she is the bean sí and the sidhe of the hollow hills; in Scotland the same who haunts the loch and the hill; in Wales she is the fair family of the woodlands; and in Cornwall the little folk of the mines. All of them carry the same deep ideas of the fairy world and of the care humans must take with the Otherworld.
